narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The earliest mention of the Furry Dance appears in a 1790 letter to the Gentleman's Magazine, describing it as a custom dedicated to 'revelry' on May 8th.
The event is linked to the feast of the Apparition of the Archangel Michael, Helston's patron saint.
on_screen: Map: United Kingdom · Europe

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance celebrates the passing of winter and the arrival of spring.
It is held on May 8th, or the preceding Saturday if that date falls on a Sunday or Monday.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is provided by the Helston Town Band.
The tune is sometimes referred to as 'John the Bone.' It is played from memory and has been recorded by various groups, including a 1943 BBC recording.
Listen for the Brass band.
A brass band performance, traditionally played from memory, associated with the town's spring festivities.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Katie Moss, a composer who wrote 'The Floral Dance' in 1911; Robert Morton Nance, who added the Saint Michael verse to the Hal-an-Tow in the 1930s.
Similar customs include the 'Schärensprung' in Biewer, Germany, and the 'Obby 'Oss festival in Padstow, Cornwall.

images.attribution: Rod Allday / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 2.0
images.description: Coinagehall Street Helston : The Hal an Tow celebration arriving. Hal an Tow takes place early in the morning on Flora Day. It is a medieval play depicting the arrival of St Piran bringing Christianity to Cornwall, the slaying of the dragon by St George and the slaying of the devil by Helston's saint, St Michael. 'Hellys bys vykken' seen on the banner is Cornish for 'Helston for ever'.

images.attribution: Steve G / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 2.0
Rod Allday / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 2.0
images.description: Coinagehall Street Helston The 8 o'clock dance on Flora Day 2009.  Flora Day is an ancient rite of spring which occurs on 8th May every year (or the nearest Saturday if the 8th falls on Sunday or Monday market day).  Various dances take place throughout the day, passing through the town and this is the first dance of the day.
